LESSONS.title: Reading an address
LESSONS.goal: Split an address (URL) to get the server, path and search words
summary: Address = scheme + server + path + query
urlparse splits an address into parts
parse_qs turns a query into a dictionary

cards.say: A web address (URL) is made of parts. https is the scheme, ria.example is the server name, /bus is the path, and ?s=101 is the query (the question you're asking). urlparse splits the parts for you.
cards.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
p = urlparse(input())
print(p.netloc)
print(p.path)

cards.say: A query looks like name=value. When parse_qs makes a dictionary, each value comes in a list, so add [0] to take out the first value.
cards.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
from urllib.parse import parse_qs
url = input()
d = parse_qs(urlparse(url).query)
print(d["s"][0])

items.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
p = urlparse(input())
print(p.path)
items.explain: path is the part after the server name and before the ?. The server name is netloc, and what comes after the question mark is query.

items.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
p = urlparse(input())
print(p.query)
items.explain: query holds the name=value part without the question mark. To get just the value, use parse_qs.

items.code:
from urllib.parse import parse_qs
d = parse_qs(input())
print(d["day"][0])
items.explain: parse_qs puts each value in a list. ["day"] takes out the list, and [0] takes out the first value inside it.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the server name ria.example is printed.
items.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
p = urlparse(input())
print(p.___)
items.explain: The server name is netloc. path gives /menu, and query gives an empty line because this address has no query.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the server name and then the path are printed.
items.explain: import comes first. Split the address into p, then take parts out of p. The server name is printed first.

items.task: Get an address with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Use urlparse and parse_qs to take out the q value and print “Search: value”. Example: https://ria.example/search?q=coffee → Search: coffee
items.starter:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
from urllib.parse import parse_qs
url = input()
hints: Each address has q in a different spot with a different value. Where is q in the second address?
Take out just the query part of the address with urlparse, then turn it into a dictionary with parse_qs.
Use the "q" key to get the list from the dictionary, pick its first value and print it with the label.

d = parse_qs(urlparse(url).query)
print("Search:", d["q"][___])
items.solution:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
from urllib.parse import parse_qs
url = input()
d = parse_qs(urlparse(url).query)
print("Search:", d["q"][0])
items.explain: urlparse cut off the query and parse_qs made a dictionary. The nice part: the same code works whether q comes first or last.

items.q: In https://ria.example/bus?s=101, which part is s=101?
items.explain: The name=value after the question mark is the query. The server name is ria.example, and the path is /bus.

LESSONS.title: Requests and responses
LESSONS.goal: Send a request with urlopen and handle the response and errors
summary: urlopen → read().decode()
Status code 200 success, 404 not found
HTTPError first, URLError after

cards.say: Real code sends a request to a server on the internet. Here, a practice server answers instead. Send a request with urlopen, and turn the data you get into a string with read().decode().
cards.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/menu"
with urlopen(url) as r:
    print(r.status)
    print(r.read().decode())

cards.say: Status codes 400 and up, like 404 (page not found) and 500 (server problem), raise HTTPError. If the server can't be found, it's URLError. Put except HTTPError first.
cards.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.error import URLError
url = input()
try:
    urlopen(url)
    print("Success")
except HTTPError as e:
    print("Code", e.code)
except URLError:
    print("Connection failed")

items.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/menu"
with urlopen(url) as r:
    print(r.status)
items.explain: The menu page answers normally, so the status code is 200. 200 is the agreed number for “success”.

items.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
url = "https://ria.example/old"
try:
    urlopen(url)
except HTTPError as e:
    print(e.code)
items.explain: A missing page answers with a code of 400 or more, and Python reports it as HTTPError. e.code holds that number.
There's no server called closed.example in the practice table (the server can't be found), so no response comes back at all: URLError. If a server answers with an error code, it's HTTPError.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the data you got is printed as a string.
items.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/menu"
with urlopen(url) as r:
    print(r.read().___())
items.explain: read() gives you bytes. decode() turns them into a string, and with empty parentheses it reads UTF-8. Bytes have no encode, so that's an AttributeError, and split prints a list of byte pieces.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the body of the address you enter is printed.
items.explain: After the import, open the request and, inside it, turn the body into a string and store it in text. Once it's stored, show it with print.

items.task: Get an address with input() (leave the parentheses empty), connect with urlopen and print the body. On HTTPError print “Error code N”, and on URLError print “Connection failed”. Example: https://ria.example/menu → Americano 3000 won
items.starter:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.error import URLError
url = input()
hints: Depending on the address you get a body, an error code or a connection failure. Which address gives which?
Put the request that might fail inside try, and write a separate except for each kind of error.
Inside try, open the request, turn the body into a string and print it. HTTPError uses e.code, and URLError prints a message.
items.solution:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.error import URLError
url = input()
try:
    with urlopen(url) as r:
        print(r.read().decode())
except HTTPError as e:
    print("Error code", e.code)
except URLError:
    print("Connection failed")
items.explain: Writing HTTPError first and URLError after is the right order. HTTPError is a kind of URLError, so if you swap them, URLError catches it first and the error code is never printed.

options: There's no page at that address
items.explain: 404 means “not found”, 200 is success, and 500 is a problem on the server side. Knowing what the numbers mean helps you guess an error's cause fast.

LESSONS.title: Reading HTML
LESSONS.goal: Find and take out the text you want from a response body
summary: HTML is just one long string too
You can take parts out with find and slicing
re takes out the text between tags

cards.say:
A web page (HTML) is text wrapped in tags, like

Title

. To Python it's just a long string, so find and slicing can take out what's between the tags.
cards.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen url = "https://ria.example/cafe" with urlopen(url) as r: html = r.read().decode() start = html.find("

") + 4 end = html.find("

") print(html[start:end])

cards.say: With re, wrap [^<]+ (several characters that aren't <) in parentheses and group(1) gives it to you. Our practice HTML is simple, so this is enough, but real projects use an HTML parser.
cards.code:
import re from urllib.request import urlopen url = "https://ria.example/cafe" with urlopen(url) as r: html = r.read().decode() pat = r"

([^<]+)

" m = re.search(pat, html) print(m.group(1))

items.code:
html = "

Cafe

" print(html.find(""))
items.explain:
takes indexes 0–3 and Cafe 4–7, so

starts at index 8.

items.code:
import re html = "

3000 won

" html += "

4500 won

" pat = r"

([^<]+)

" m = re.search(pat, html) print(m.group(1))
items.explain: search returns only the first match. group(1) takes out just the 3000 won inside the parentheses.

items.code:
import re html = "

3000 won

" html += "

4500 won

" pat = r"

([^<]+)

" print(re.findall(pat, html))
items.explain: findall finds them all and gives a list. If the pattern has parentheses, only the text inside them goes in.

items.q: Fill in the blank so all the menu items found are printed as a list.
items.code: import re html = "CoffeeBread" pat = r"([^<]+)" print(re.___(pat, html))
items.explain: findall is the one that finds them all and returns a list. sub replaces text, so it's missing arguments and causes an error, and split gives different pieces.

items.q: Put the lines in order so only the title text is printed.
items.explain:
Cut at and keep the front part as head, then drop the four characters of

and the title is left. Print title last.

items.task: Get an address with input() (leave the parentheses empty) and connect with urlopen. Take out the text inside h1 and inside the first p, and print “h1 - p”. Example: https://ria.example/cafe → Sunflower Cafe - 3000 won
items.starter:
import re
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = input()
hints: Each page has a different title and price. The third page has two p tags. Which one do you use?
After turning the body into text, you can take out what's between tags with find and slicing, or with re.
Take out the h1 text and the first p text, then print them with “ - ” in between.

with urlopen(url) as r: html = r.read().decode() t = re.search(r"

([^<]+)

", html) p = re.search(___, html) print(t.group(1), "-", p.group(1))
items.solution:
import re from urllib.request import urlopen url = input() with urlopen(url) as r: html = r.read().decode() pt = r"

([^<]+)

" pp = r"

([^<]+)

" t = re.search(pt, html) p = re.search(pp, html) print(t.group(1), "-", p.group(1))
items.explain: search returns only the first match, so even on the page with two p tags you get the first price. Change only the address and the same code reads it.

items.q: To Python, what is an HTML response?
items.explain: Once decode() has turned it into text, HTML is just a string. That's why string tools like find, slicing and re work on it.

LESSONS.title: Reading many pages
LESSONS.goal: Collect links and read many pages with a loop
summary: findall collects the href links
for follows the links one by one
Missing pages are skipped with HTTPError

cards.say: A list page has links (href) to other pages. Collect all the links with findall and you get a list.
cards.code:
import re
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = input()
with urlopen(url) as r:
    html = r.read().decode()
pat = r'href="([^"]+)"'
print(re.findall(pat, html))

cards.say: Loop over the link list with for, put the server address in front and connect to each one. Take the title out of each page and print it on its own line.
cards.code:
import re from urllib.request import urlopen base = "https://ria.example" pat = r"

([^<]+)

" for link in ["/c1", "/c2"]: with urlopen(base + link) as r: html = r.read().decode() m = re.search(pat, html) print(m.group(1))

items.code:
import re
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = input()
with urlopen(url) as r:
    html = r.read().decode()
pat = r'href="([^"]+)"'
print(re.findall(pat, html))
items.explain: The list has three links. findall puts only the text in parentheses, the link addresses, into the list.
A link only has the path, so you put the server address in front to get a full address. The loop runs twice, so two lines come out.
/f1 is fine, so “Found”. /f3 is a 404, so HTTPError happens and except prints “Missing”. Even with an error, the loop keeps going.

items.q: Fill in the blank so each link is printed one by one.
items.code:
import re
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = input()
with urlopen(url) as r:
    html = r.read().decode()
pat = r'href="([^"]+)"'
for link in re.___(pat, html):
    print(link)
items.explain: for goes well with findall, which returns a list. search and match give one result or None, so you can't loop over them and it causes an error.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the two page addresses are printed in turn.
items.explain: Make base first, then loop with for and build and print the address inside. The two lines inside the loop are indented, so they run every time.

items.task: Get a list address with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Find all the href links in the list, put each after https://ria.example with for, connect with urlopen and print the h1 title. For a missing page (HTTPError), print “No title”. Example: /list/cafe → two lines
items.starter:
import re
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
base = "https://ria.example"
url = input()

tests.expect:
Gimbap House
Snack Bar
No title

hints: Each list has a different number of links. What happens to the last link in the food list?
Read the list page first and collect the links with findall, then loop over that list with for.
Inside the loop, join the server address and the link, connect and print the h1 title. Wrap the connection in try.
items.solution:
import re from urllib.request import urlopen from urllib.error import HTTPError base = "https://ria.example" url = input() with urlopen(url) as r: html = r.read().decode() pl = r'href="([^"]+)"' pt = r"

([^<]+)

" for link in re.findall(pl, html): try: u = base + link with urlopen(u) as r: page = r.read().decode() except HTTPError: print("No title") else: m = re.search(pt, page) print(m.group(1))
items.explain: You collected links and followed them with for, and except skipped the missing page so the loop never broke. It works for a list with just one link, too.

items.q: Which keyword do you use to follow a list of links one by one?
items.explain: Handling the items of a list one by one is the for loop's job. Even if more links show up, you don't need to change the code.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 13 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Read an address, send a request and pull out information
summary: urlparse splits an address
urlopen, status codes, error handling
Pull info from many pages with re and for

cards.say: Time to wrap up Chapter 13. You read addresses, sent requests, handled errors and pulled info out of the body. Let's finish with a program that reads a weather page.
cards.code:
import re from urllib.request import urlopen url = input() with urlopen(url) as r: html = r.read().decode() pat = r"

([^<]+)

" m = re.search(pat, html) print(m.group(1))

items.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
p = urlparse(input())
print(p.query)
items.explain: Everything after the question mark is the query. /bus is the path, and 101 is a value you only get by taking it out with parse_qs.

items.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
url = "https://ria.example/oops"
try:
    urlopen(url)
except HTTPError as e:
    print(e.code)
items.explain: The oops page answers with 500, which means a server problem. It's 400 or more, so it's HTTPError, and the number is in e.code.
The server gone.example can't be found, so there's no response: URLError. HTTPError only happens when a server answers with a code of 400 or more.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the second p's text, Sunny, is printed.
items.code:
import re html = "

18C

Sunny

" pat = r"

([^<]+)

" print(re.findall(pat, html)[___])
items.explain: The findall list is ['18C', 'Sunny']. Numbering starts at 0, so the second one is 1. 2 is out of range and gives an IndexError.

items.code: html = "Tea" print(html.find(""))
items.explain: takes indexes 0–2 and Tea 3–5, so starts at 6. find tells you the index where it found the text.

items.q: Put the lines in order so addresses are built from the links and printed.
items.explain: Put the server address first, then inside for, join the link to build the address and print it. The two inner lines are indented.

items.task: Get an address with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Take out the city, the temperature (it can be negative) and the weather, and print “Seoul: 18C, Sunny”. Turn the temperature into an int, and if it's 5°C or less add “ (Bundle up!)” at the end. On HTTPError print “City not found”.
items.starter:
import re
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
url = input()
hints: Each city has a different temperature and weather. Does exactly 5 get “Bundle up!”? And what happens to mars?
Wrap the connection in try to catch HTTPError, then take out the h1 and the two p tags from the body with re.
Turn the temperature into an int and compare it with 5. Build the text, then add the ending if the condition holds. Put the minus sign in the pattern too.

pt = r"Temp (-?\d+)C"
temp = int(re.search(pt, html).group(1))
text = f"{city}: {temp}C, {sky}"
if temp <= ___:
    text += " (Bundle up!)"
items.solution:
import re from urllib.request import urlopen from urllib.error import HTTPError url = input() p1 = r"

([^<]+)

" p2 = r"Temp (-?\d+)C" p3 = r"

([^<]+)

" try: with urlopen(url) as r: html = r.read().decode() except HTTPError: print("City not found") else: c = re.search(p1, html) city = c.group(1) m = re.search(p2, html) temp = int(m.group(1)) sky = re.findall(p3, html)[1] text = f"{city}: {temp}C, {sky}" if temp <= 5: text += " (Bundle up!)" print(text)
items.explain: You joined it all: reading the address, requesting, handling errors and pulling out info. One program handles the edge case of 5, below-zero temperatures and even a missing city. Congrats on finishing this chapter!

items.q: Between HTTPError and URLError, which except do you write first?
items.explain: HTTPError is a kind of URLError. If you write URLError first, HTTPError gets caught there too, and you never get to use e.code.

ADVANCED.title: Sending values in a request
ADVANCED.goal: Add ?name=value to an address and get a different response for each value
summary: Send a value with ?name=value after the address
Join several values with &
The practice server answers only an exact match

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. In 13-1 you read ?s=101 in an address, right? This time you add ?item=value yourself and send the request.
cards.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
base = "https://ria.example/price"
url = base + "?item=" + input()
with urlopen(url) as r:
    print(r.read().decode())

cards.say: For two or more values, join them with &. The practice server answers only addresses that match exactly, order included. (Real servers usually don't care about the order.) For now, use only English letters and numbers in values (14-4 shows how to send spaces and letters like é).
cards.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
base = "https://ria.example/price"
q = "?item=tea&size=big"
with urlopen(base + q) as r:
    print(r.read().decode())

items.code:
base = "https://ria.example/price"
url = base + "?item=" + "tea"
print(url)
items.explain: You joined "?item=" and the value to the address text with +. ? starts the query, and item=tea is the name=value.

items.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse
from urllib.parse import parse_qs
base = "https://ria.example/price"
url = base + "?item=tea&size=big"
d = parse_qs(urlparse(url).query)
print(d["size"][0])
items.explain: Read the query you added back with parse_qs and you get big, the value of size. Values come in a list, so take it out with [0].

items.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import URLError
base = "https://ria.example/price"
q = "?size=big&item=tea"
try:
    urlopen(base + q)
    print("Success")
except URLError:
    print("Connection failed")
items.explain: The practice server's table only has addresses with item first and size after. With the order swapped, the text is different, so there's no response and you get URLError. A real server would usually answer either way.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the query starts.
items.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
base = "https://ria.example/price"
url = base + "___item=" + input()
with urlopen(url) as r:
    print(r.read().decode())
items.explain: A query starts with ?. & only joins the second value onward, so here it makes a different address, and / turns it into a different path. Either way, the server can't answer.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the request address for the menu item you enter is printed.
items.explain: Make the query piece q first, put it after the server address to make url, then print it. You need q before you can make url.

items.task: Get item and then size with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Add ?item=…&size=… after base, send the request and print “item size: body”. If it's sold out (HTTPError), print “item size: Sold out”. Example: latte, big → latte big: 4500 won
items.starter:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
base = "https://ria.example/price"
item = input()
size = input()
hints: Enter a different item or size and the server's response changes. The values you enter have to go into the address.
Join ?item=value&size=value with + to build the address. item comes first.
Send a request to the address you built and read the body. Catch the sold-out case with except HTTPError and print different text.
items.solution:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
base = "https://ria.example/price"
item = input()
size = input()
url = base + "?item=" + item
url = url + "&size=" + size
try:
    with urlopen(url) as r:
        body = r.read().decode()
except HTTPError:
    body = "Sold out"
print(f"{item} {size}: {body}")
items.explain: You added the input to the query to build the address, and the same code got a different response for each item and size. You handled sold out separately, too.

items.q: When you add two values to a query, which characters go before the first value and between the two?
items.explain: ? is written once, at the start of the query, and values are joined with &. Example: ?item=tea&size=big.

ADVANCED.title: Handling each status code
ADVANCED.goal: Give different messages depending on the status code number
summary: 400s are request problems, 500s are server problems
Split e.code with if/elif
Every code starting with 2 is a success

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. In 13-2 you caught HTTPError, right? You can branch on the e.code number. 404 is a missing page, and the 500s are server errors.
Success isn't only 200. Anything starting with 2, like 201, is a success and passes without an error. Check the number with r.status.
cards.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = input()
with urlopen(url) as r:
    if r.status == 201:
        print("Newly created")
    else:
        print("Plain success")

items.explain: busy answers with 503. It's not 404 and it's 500 or more, so the second branch, “Server error”, is printed.
404 is also 400 or more, so it's caught by the first condition. elif is only checked when the one before is false, so “No such page” can never come out. Put the narrower condition first.

items.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
url = "https://ria.example/shop/new"
with urlopen(url) as r:
    print(r.status)
items.explain: 201, which means something new was created, also starts with 2, so it's a success. It isn't an error, so it doesn't go to except, and r.status holds the number.

items.q: Fill in the cutoff number so 403 goes to “Check request”.
items.explain: 403 is in the 400s, so it's a problem with your request. With a cutoff of 500, 403 falls to the else. With 400 or 300, 403 would wrongly count as a server error too.

items.q: Put the lines in order so the first digit (2) of the success code is printed.
items.explain: Open the request, store the status code in a variable inside it, then print the quotient of dividing by 100. 201 // 100 is 2, so you can tell it's a success.

items.task: Get an address with input() (leave the parentheses empty). On success print “Success” and the code. For 404 print “No such page”, for other 400s “Bad request” and the code, and for 500s “Server error” and the code. Example: /shop/new → Success 201
items.starter:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
url = input()
hints: Each address has a different status code. There are four branches: success, 404, other 400s and 500s.
For success, get the number from r.status inside try. For errors, get it from e.code in except HTTPError as e.
Inside except, check 404 first, then 500 or more, then the rest, split with if/elif/else.
items.explain: The success code shows r.status as it is, so 201 was right too. Errors split in the order 404, 500s, the rest, so the 403 and 500 edges were right as well.

options: A problem on the server side
items.explain: The 500s are server-side problems. The 400s mean the request was wrong, and codes starting with 2 are successes.

ADVANCED.title: Collecting many pages
ADVANCED.goal: Count up page numbers, read to the end, collect and summarize
summary: Request with ?page= going up by 1
break when a missing page (404) comes up
Collect each page's values in a list

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. In 13-4 you followed links, right? This time you count the page number up by one. When a missing page (404) comes up, that's the end.
cards.code:
from urllib.request import urlopen
from urllib.error import HTTPError
base = "https://ria.example/news"
page = 1
while True:
    url = base + "?page=" + str(page)
    try:
        urlopen(url)
    except HTTPError:
        break
    print("Page", page, "exists")
    page += 1
cards.out:
Page 1 exists
Page 2 exists
Page 3 exists

cards.say: Take the prices out of each page and collect them in a list. After the loop, get the count with len and the total with sum to summarize in one go.
cards.code:

items.solution:
import re from urllib.request import urlopen from urllib.error import HTTPError base = input() pat = r"

(\d+)

" prices = [] page = 1 while True: url = base + "?page=" + str(page) try: with urlopen(url) as r: html = r.read().decode() except HTTPError: break for p in re.findall(pat, html): prices.append(int(p)) page += 1 pages = page - 1 n = len(prices) total = sum(prices) a = f"Pages {pages}, prices {n}," print(a, f"total {total} won")
items.explain: You counted up page numbers, stopped at the 404, and collected and summarized the values. Boards with just one page or none at all ended correctly too.

items.q: When you don't know how many pages there are, how do you end the loop?
options: break on the missing page's HTTPError
Loop without except until an error stops it
items.explain: A missing page answers with 404, and Python raises HTTPError. If you break then, you read exactly to the end and stop, even without knowing the page count.
